newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian soldier heads home from Chechen captivity.
newsitem.headline: Russian soldier heads home from Chechen captivity.

text.p: Tuesday was a special day for Anatoly Kovin. After half a year of captivity in breakaway Chechnya the 19-year-old Russian conscript was going home.
"I am very happy, I just want to see my family again," said Kovin, who was taken captive last June in mountains near the village of Vedeno by rebel guerrillas battling Russian troops.

Local chief of police Shaman Abbazov formally handed Kovin over on Tuesday to representatives of the Memorial organisation, which is working to release soldiers still in captivity after the Chechen conflict.

"Anatoly's release is an act of goodwill with no conditions attached. The Chechen side has acted in this way many times," Abbazov told Reuters. "We wish Russia would show the same goodwill towards Chechen prisoners of war."

A peace agreement was signed last August putting a halt to nearly two years of fierce fighting in the Caucasian region, but the two sides have made little progress in releasing captives and they disagree about the numbers involved.

Moscow, whose troops fought to keep Chechnya inside the Russian Federation, says many soldiers are held prisoner by the separatists. Chechen sources say they have about 20 captives but some 2,500 of their compatriots are being held in Russia.
Russia pulled its last remaining troops out of Chechnya earlier this month ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections in the region set for January 27.

"The Russian authorities don't even seem bothered about seeking the freedom of their own people," said Abbazov, whose white-washed office is decorated with verses from the Koran in Arabic script and a picture of a mosque.
He said Kovin was the last Russian captive in the Vedeno area, which lies south of the Chechen capital Grozny and is a stronghold of guerrilla leader and now presidential candidate Shamil Basayev.
Kovin, slightly-built and wearing a denim jacket, said the Chechens had taken good care of him. He seemed completely at ease, joking and laughing with the young Chechens guarding him.
He said some of the guerrillas had tried to convert him to Islam and he had not drunk alcohol for six months.

Kovin spent the first few months of captivity living with the rebel guerrillas, moving from place to place, but was then moved to a village. He whiled away his time reading, listening to the radio and learning some of the Chechen language.
He said he was initially kept with other Russian captives, adding that he thought they had all now been released.
"I never doubted they would release me (too) when the time was right," he said.
Kovin said he had not been in contact with his family at all during his captivity and that his parents did not know whether he was dead or alive.
Emran Abzyev, deputy president of Memorial in Chechnya, will drive Kovin some 2,000 km (1,300 miles) to his home in Siberia.
"There he can study, work, resume a normal life again," said Abzyev.
Abzyev said some Russians, particularly those who deserted during their time in Chechnya, were too frightened to go home.
Police chief Abbazov shook Kovin's hand and said, in a paternal tone: "Remember, Anatoly, be a man, be a human being.
"And keep off the booze," he added with a laugh.
